changes.after: Editing C source changes the instructions on disk. Build again to put those changes into the program you run.

before: A C compiler translates source and a linker combines compiled parts into an executable. These examples use an implementation that provides the standard library.
int main(void) is the entry function here. void in its parameter list means no arguments; returning zero reports successful termination to the host.
Editing main.c does not alter an already-built executable. Recompile before expecting a changed source value to appear.
This course uses portable C17 core rules. C23 is newer, but the installed GCC 14.2 describes its C23 support as incomplete. No browser C runner is provided.
Expected output or behavior: Ready. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: In a new disposable folder save main.c, run gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic main.c -o lesson, then ./lesson. Edit the message; compare running before and after rebuilding. Do not overwrite another project. You may trace it without a C compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: Source is the text you write. A compiler translates it into machine instructions. A linker joins the compiled parts and library tools into an executable: a program you can run.
In this example, main is the starting function. `void` means it takes no inputs. Returning 0 from main reports a successful finish.
Changing main.c does not change an executable you already built. Build again to include the new instructions. Otherwise, running the old executable can still show the old message.
These lessons use C17, a version of the C language rules. C23 is newer, but you do not need its features for this course. The app shows and explains code; it does not run C.
This program prints Ready on one line. Saving different text in the source will not change this result until you rebuild.

Optional local practice: save the example as main.c in a new folder. With GCC installed, build it using `gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic main.c -o lesson`. On Linux or macOS, run `./lesson`; in Windows PowerShell, run `.\lesson.exe`. Change the message, then compare the result before and after rebuilding.

before.question: You edit the message but run the old executable without rebuilding. Which outcome is possible?
choices: Saving source always rebuilds the executable.
The executable reads the source text on every run.
before.explanation: The executable contains the previous compilation, separate from the edited source.

after.question: You edit the message but run the old program without rebuilding. What can happen?
choices: Saving the source always rebuilds the program.
The built program reads main.c every time.
after.explanation: The old program still contains the old instructions. A new build is needed to include your edit.
